Christmas Eve.
Dear diary, I feel bad. Elizabeth, my big cousin, was in charge of the nativity play at Grandma's house, and she told me to tell little Rosie she couldn't be an angel because she ruins everything. I didn't want to. Rosie is only five and had her tinsel halo ready. But Elizabeth is sixteen and bossy and said, 'Just do it, Thomas. I'm the director.' So I did. Rosie cried behind the curtain. I told myself it wasn't my fault, Elizabeth decided. But I was the one who said it. My tummy hurt all through dinner. Thomas

passage: You asked about being a teaching assistant. I'm Harish, and I'll be honest: it brought out something ugly. They gave me a badge and the power to mark first-year lab records. My professor saw the zero, checked the record and called me in. 'Harish, would you treat your cousin like this?' That question stayed with me. I rechecked every record I'd failed. Most were fine. Kalyani

passage: In the tailor's shop in the town of Bhadrachalam, Lakshmi had been 'the helper' for a year. Madhav Anna, the master tailor, never let her cut cloth; she swept threads, ironed and fetched tea. Customers spoke over her head to him. At first she practised cutting on old newspaper at night, dreaming of her own shop. By the monsoon she had stopped. When a customer asked her something about a blouse pattern, she said, 'Ask Anna,' though she knew the answer better than he did. She was starting to believe she was only good for sweeping. One evening her younger sister found the newspaper patterns under the bed. 'These are so good. Why did you stop?' Lakshmi shrugged, then felt a hot flash of resentment, not at her sister, at the whole year. 'Because everyone treats me like the helper,' she said. 'And I started to believe them.'

passage: I'm Parul, and I've known Hemant since school; he's the one who cries at weddings and feeds every street dog in our lane. Last month he got a job supervising the loading bay at a warehouse, and I started in the office upstairs. From the window I watched him. He shouted at the loaders for a two-minute break, docked a man's pay for a torn sack, made an old worker restack in the heat while he watched. At home he's gentle. At the bay, in that orange vest with the whistle, he's someone else. I didn't gossip. On Sunday, over his mother's poha, I said, 'You know, at work you're not how you are at home. The loaders are scared of you.' He looked stung, then quiet. 'The manager says if I'm soft, they'll walk all over me.' 'Maybe. But you're not soft here, and nobody walks over you.'

January: Tanvir's flatmate Joseph started as night supervisor of the security team at a Kochi mall. At home he still hummed while cooking and apologised to the cat.
March: Tanvir went to pick him up after a late film and saw Joseph at the gate, barking at a young guard who had dozed off, making him stand to attention in front of shoppers, calling him useless. The guard's ears were red. Tanvir almost didn't recognise his friend's voice. He felt a flash of anger, then something softer. He waited.
The next Sunday: over breakfast, Tanvir said carefully, 'Can I tell you something odd? At the mall the other night you weren't like you are here. That guard looked scared of you.' Joseph put down his fork. 'They told me the job needs a hard face.' 'Maybe firm. But you called him useless in front of everyone.' Joseph was quiet for a long time. 'I'll talk to him tomorrow.'

passage: Chandrika, you're worried about your friend who became a school discipline officer and turned harsh. Let me tell you about my friend Gopal. At twenty-five he became a ticket inspector on the Mumbai locals. At home Gopal was the softest man I knew; he carried his mother's shopping and sang to his nieces. On the trains, in that black coat, he became another person: shouting at labourers without tickets, making a fisherwoman get off at the wrong station, laughing with the other inspectors about 'these people'. I watched it happen over a year. I didn't gossip, though others did. One evening at his house I said, 'Gopal, the man in the black coat isn't you. You're the one who sings to your nieces.' He was angry, then silent. Months later he told me he had started letting the old fisherwomen ride to their stop. Mridul's lesson, beta: speak to the person, not the coat.

passage: Lavanya, you've just become warden and I can see you stiffening already, so let me tell you about my first year. I was twenty-five, warden of a girls' hostel in Coimbatore. One night I shouted at a student who had come back late from visiting her grandmother in hospital. She cried, and I felt powerful. Then on the bus home I thought: Shalini, would you speak to your own niece like this? No. So I did three things. I asked the principal to sit in on one hostel meeting a month. I put a box in the mess for anonymous complaints about me. And every Friday I ate dinner with the girls, not at the warden's table. The complaints were painful to read. passage: The monsoon was two weeks away, and the site in Pune was behind schedule. Eshaan, supervising his first crew, had started to change. Madhav Kaka stood up slowly, without a word. That silence stopped Eshaan. He thought: I'd never talk to my own grandfather like this. That evening he called the project manager and asked her to visit the site weekly and see how he ran it. The next morning he gathered the crew. 'I've been harsh. Tell me what's making the work slow.' Madhav Kaka spoke first: the cement arrived late every day, and there was no shade for breaks. Eshaan fixed both. They finished the roof four days before the rain.
